articles.title: Lewis Hamilton reveals he's 'lost out' in recent F1 races with set-up of his Ferrari car compared to Charles Leclerc
articles.summary: Lewis Hamilton feels he's not optimised set-up of his Ferrari car recently which has cost him performance; Hamilton finished fourth in Sunday's US Grand Prix while Charles Leclerc was second; watch every session of the Mexico City GP from this Friday, live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
Hamilton was outqualified by Leclerc at the United States Grand Prix and was unable to match his team-mate's impressive pace in the race on his way to fourth, while Leclerc finished second behind race-winner Kimi Antonelli.

At the previous race in Singapore, Hamilton looked strong in qualifying until Q3 when he was beaten by Leclerc, and a similar pattern occurred in Austin where the seven-time world champion topped final practice, only to qualify fifth.

"I lost a lot of points in the last five races or so," Hamilton, who is one point behind second-placed George Russell in the Drivers' Championship, told Sky Sports F1 .

"I think it has come from set-up, not perfect, the set-up. That's something I really have to get on top of. That's where I have lost out. Performance-wise I feel like I've been driving well and the last [race] stint [in Austin] was good. The first two stints there was nothing I could do about that.

"Definitely lots to take away. The team did a great job to bring an upgrade. Charles got a second place. We have got good performance. Hopefully when we go to Mexico, we can improve on where we have gone wrong on that setup."

Ferrari continued to be the benchmark team in most corners at the Circuit of the Americas but lacked straight-line speed compared to Mercedes and Red Bull.

But, Hamilton was unhappy with the car's low-speed balance in the first two stints of the Grand Prix which put him out of the podium fight.

"I lost so much time. I couldn't turn the car in the low-speed particularly - Turn 1, Turn 11, Turn 12, Turn 13, 14, 15. Massive understeer so the [other] cars pulled away when I was adjusting my settings," he said.

"By the time we got to the last stint, we got closer to the balance but we should have started with that balance at the beginning. Lots of learnings. The team did a great job with pit stops and strategy."

Could Leclerc have won United States GP?

Leclerc qualified fourth but had a superb start by overtaking Isack Hadjar and Max Verstappen in the first sector, only for Verstappen to overtake the Ferrari driver at the end of the first lap.

Ferrari opted for a two-stop strategy with Leclerc which saw him charge past Verstappen and Lando Norris, who did a one-stop race, in the closing stages but he ultimately finished 13 seconds behind Antonelli.

Leclerc believes his qualifying position cost him a chance at victory but even if he had less traffic to contend with in the race, Antonelli was "just too quick".

"If you look at FP1, FP2 and FP3, we were very strong. If you look at qualifying, at the end of the day in Q3, it was extremely difficult to bring the tyres up to temperature, and we probably lost a shot at the victory there," said Leclerc.

"But Kimi was very strong, so, as a whole weekend, I think we're just not robust enough."

Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur believes Leclerc could have won the race in different circumstances.

"The race went well - the racing went well, the pace was OK, we were aggressive with the strategy because we had to overtake," Vasseur told Sky Sports F1 .

"Overall, if we missed something it was the last two laps in Q3. That was the most important laps of the weekend and that's where we had the issue.

"Overall, I want to take the positive of the weekend that the pace was there from FP1 to the last lap of the race. Without the VSC it would have been a double podium but let's try to do a better qualifying in Mexico and win the race."

Five rounds remain in the 2026 season with the Mexico City Grand Prix up first this weekend, where altitude will be a factor given the track is 2,200m above sea level.

The performance of the Ferrari power unit at altitude will dictate if they can challenge for victory at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, which features lots of twisty corners which the SF-26 should enjoy.

"It's such fine margins, and it also depends on what the upgrade plans of the others are in upcoming races. But the feeling with the car is getting better and better," said Leclerc.

"These cars are very specific and unique, and I feel like, over the last two or three races, I've unlocked something again in terms of driving, and particularly setup with my driving. Just both together, we've taken a step forward, and I just feel much more comfortable with the car.

"I hope that this will result in a win soon. Whether it's in Singapore or in Austin, we were quite close, so I'm confident that we'll have a shot to win a race before the end of the season."

Formula 1 next heads south for the second leg of The Americas triple header with the Mexico City Grand Prix this weekend, live on Sky Sports F1. Stream Sky Sports with NOW - no contract, cancel anytime

articles.title: F1 Q&A: Antonelli dominance, Hamilton eyes Africa GP & Albon form
articles.summary: BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the United States Grand Prix.
articles.body:
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli is one step closer to becoming the new F1 world champion after winning the United States Grand Prix from pole position.

The 20-year-old Italian, who leads team-mate George Russell by 123 points in the standings, will secure the title in Mexico City on Sunday by finishing ninth or higher.

BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the race in Austin.

Antonelli delivers 'the race of a champion who isn't the champion yet'

This weekend, both Mercedes drivers had the new upgrades but Kimi Antonelli dominated qualifying and the race while George Russell didn't quite achieve the same success. There is a theme throughout the season. How much of that is down to driver ability, driving style etc and how much is down to car set-up and strategy. Is George better than this or has he reached his limit? - Julian

The dominant theme of the 2026 season has been the degree to which Kimi Antonelli has stepped up his game after a mixed rookie season that contained some definite highs, but also quite a few difficulties.

In doing so, he has overwhelmed George Russell, who has accepted and is more than willing to say that Antonelli has simply done a better job than him this season.

Antonelli's performances this year have lived up to the billing with which he came to F1 - that he could be the sport's next generational talent.

He has had some luck, and some of his wins have turned on fortune - safety cars in Japan and Madrid, for example.

But he has also performed at a level of consistent excellence, and produced some absolutely standout performances, most obviously Monaco, Monza and Austin.

The Mercedes has on average been the best car, but Antonelli is the only one of the team's two drivers who has always been a factor. He fully deserves the world title that he is almost certain to clinch this weekend in Mexico City.

As for Russell, he has fundamentally used driving style as an explanation for his relative struggles, saying the previous cars suited his, and the new ones Antonelli's. He has won only three races compared with Antonelli's nine.

On Sunday, team principal Toto Wolff said Russell had struggled in Austin to get the right set-up on the Mercedes with the new upgrade package, which has been problematic since it was introduced in Malaysia.

Wolff said: "George, for all of us in the team, is a champion and has won in every category and merits to be put in the group of the very best ones. And we've seen that last year.

"This year, we see this variability in results. When we land the car in the way that suits him, he's absolutely fine. But when it drops out of that operational window, he struggles and he struggles more than maybe Kimi. And that is on us.

"We just have to work it out with him how there can be such a difference in driving, in performance, because George is not half a second slower, three tenths slower than Kimi. That's just absolutely not the case.

"So what is it that he doesn't like? What is it that we need to do in terms of modifying the car, setting it up in a different way for him to go fast? Because it's all about the intelligence, the ability, the determination."

Driving style and set-up are genuine reasons for a driver to struggle in certain circumstances.

However, it's also a case that the absolute elite, the all-time greats - drivers such as Max Verstappen, Lewis Hamilton and Fernando Alonso - tend to find a way to be at the top of their game regardless of the car's behaviour.

The worry for Russell right now is that if Antonelli is at that level - and it looks as though he has the potential to be, given his performances in only his second season - he will have his work cut out to beat him consistently in the future.

So he needs to regroup over the winter, come back next year and prove he can get back on to Antonelli's level.

With Lewis Hamilton's intentions clear of staying in F1 until there is an African Grand Prix, which I think will most likely be with Ferrari, what does that mean for the young talents who desire to drive for Ferrari? Will it be at least another four to five years before we see new drivers replacing either or both Lewis and Charles Leclerc? - Liam

Lewis Hamilton repeated in Austin last weekend that, ideally, he would like to still be racing when Formula 1 returns to Africa.

"I'm now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that's been my dream, to be able to race in Africa," he said.

"So, yes, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we'll keep it going."

Whether he can manage to stay that long is another question.

Formula 1 has said the African Grand Prix in Rwanda will be held in the "early 2030s".

The aim is for that to be in 2030 but it's not clear whether the new track will be ready by then.

Even if they make that deadline, will Hamilton still be racing? He will be 45 at the start of 2030. That's the same age as Fernando Alonso is now, and he is still going strong.

Hamilton's answer alludes to his current contract, which it is believed lasts until the end of 2027. So he would need to do another one of three years to make it to 2030.

As he says, if he is still performing at the level he is now by the middle of next year, why not? But as yet it's not clear what Ferrari will think about that.

Hamilton's presence - and the long-term contract held by team-mate Charles Leclerc - does raise questions about Ferrari's driver academy.

First and foremost, those questions surround Oliver Bearman, who is yet to finalise his new contract with Haas for next season.

Bearman has had a strong season and a new deal is believed to be pretty much a formality - driver and team have expressed their desire to stay together, and the Briton was talking in a BBC 5 live interview at the weekend very much as if he would still be a Haas driver next year .

But Bearman has higher ambitions than staying at Haas for the rest of his career.

If Hamilton and Leclerc are going to be at Ferrari for the next four years, Bearman would have every right to be asking the team what that means for him.

If he isn't going to get into the senior team, what can they do to further his career? Do they let him go, so he can pursue his ambitions elsewhere, or do they allow him to do that while still maintaining links?

These questions become even more pressing for Bearman now Brazilian Rafael Camara - also a Ferrari young driver - is joining Haas for 2027.

Bearman needs to beat the Brazilian if he is not to face an existential threat to his future as a potential driver for a top team.

Antonelli superb and Leclerc close to perfect - driver ratings

What's been happening with Alex Albon this season? Williams team-mate Carlos Sainz seems to have the better of him, and the car doesn't look to be in a good place. - David

Of the two Williams drivers, in a team that is struggling, Carlos Sainz has had the better season.

But it's not as stark as it perhaps appears just looking on the surface.

Sainz leads Albon by two points in the championship, and while the qualifying comparison is skewed heavily towards Sainz on a head-to-head basis at 13-5, the time gap between them is 0.115 seconds.

As if Albon was not already having a rough season, to top it he incurred the wrath of Fernando Alonso in Austin after the two collided on the first lap, leaving both with damaged cars.

Alonso said: "The quality of the drivers in the lower third of the grid is very low, as we saw today with Alex."

Williams are in such a state this year that comparing the drivers should be treated with a degree of qualification.

The car has been slow, and the team have struggled with consistency between parts, as well as quality and degradation.

In other words, two parts that should perform the same have not always done so, and some of them wear out and lose performance quicker than others.

Of course that works across both drivers but it does make comparisons difficult.

Albon was asked about the comparison with Sainz in qualifying in Monza last month.

He pointed out that the crash he had in Canada when he hit a groundhog had been costly because there was a new engine in the car that weekend, which was written off. That meant he had to run an old engine longer than ideal.

And he alluded to Williams suffering from the same issues with varying engine performance that happened in the early days of the new engine rules at Mercedes and McLaren.

"There's a few things," Albon said. "In the beginning of the year, it was very battery-dominated.

"If you think even just the George and Kimi situation, that's the manufacturer side of it having issues. So you can imagine it's not just them two that have had problems.

"There's been a few qualifying sessions where the corners have been good, but you don't see it in the lap time. It's on the stopwatch.

"And then we're also going through our own issues as a team. And that's not just on my side. There's also a side where to say that both cars are performing in the same way would not be true. We've been fighting some inconsistencies in the cars that's been there since the beginning of the year.

"We're much better now at getting on top of them. If you look at the last four or five weekends, we're actually very close in terms of performance. But it's taken a while to get there."

Do you foresee a world in which live F1 coverage ever returns to free-to-air telly in the UK or is it now stuck behind a paywall for eternity? I've now taken a different career path but becoming an engineer in F1 was my ultimate ambition when I was applying for university in the early 2010s, inspired by BBC's live coverage. - Ian

In the UK, the current situation is that Sky has exclusive rights to broadcast F1 behind a paywall, while Channel 4 has highlights on free-to-air television, with live coverage of the British Grand Prix.

Sky has the rights until the end of 2034, after it struck a new deal for a larger fee earlier this year.

That came in the wake of Apple buying the US rights starting from this season.

At the same time, the television market is in flux as streaming becomes increasingly prevalent as a means of consuming content.

In that context, as well as the wider sports broadcast situation, it's hard to imagine a situation where F1 could return fully to free-to-air television.

The wider picture is it is still on free-to-air in some countries - Brazil as an example.

But F1 would also argue free-to-air does not always mean more people getting sight of the sport, depending on how it's promoted in various ways, and viewing habits are not the same in all countries.

Social media output is also an important consideration. At the same time, F1 is a business that exists to make money.

Send us your question for F1 correspondent Andrew Benson

articles.title: IMSA IS PUTTING ON SOME OF THE BEST RACING IN AMERICA — AND MOTORSPORTS FANS ARE SLEEPING ON IT! 🏁🔥
articles.summary: If you are looking for the most underrated racing series in America, it might be time to give IMSA its flowers. Sports-car racing has everything motorsports...
articles.body:
If you are looking for the most underrated racing series in America, it might be time to give IMSA its flowers.

Sports-car racing has everything motorsports fans claim they want: multiple classes fighting for position, manufacturers battling for bragging rights, legendary endurance events and races where strategy can be just as important as outright speed.

And the 2026 season finale at Road Atlanta delivered a reminder of exactly why IMSA deserves a bigger spotlight.

The 29th annual Motul Petit Le Mans brought 54 cars to Michelin Raceway Road Atlanta for 10 hours of competition on Oct. 3.

The headline belonged to Porsche Penske Motorsport. Laurens Vanthoor, Kévin Estre and Matt Campbell guided the No. 6 Porsche 963 to the overall victory, giving Porsche its first overall Petit Le Mans win with a prototype.

That is a major achievement for one of sports-car racing's most successful manufacturers.

But the race was about more than one manufacturer celebrating. Championship battles were unfolding throughout the field, with different classes producing their own fights for position and strategy.

That is IMSA's secret weapon: There is almost always something happening somewhere on the track.

Porsche took the finale, but Cadillac finished the season with the biggest championship prize.

Jack Aitken secured the GTP drivers' championship in the No. 31 Cadillac Whelen V-Series.R, becoming the first solo champion in IMSA's top class since 2009.

Cadillac also secured the GTP team and manufacturer championships.

That is the kind of season-long battle that deserves attention. One manufacturer can win the final race, while another walks away with the championship after delivering the consistency required across an entire calendar.

In endurance racing, speed matters. So does reliability, execution and surviving the moments when everything threatens to fall apart.

Formula 1 has its global superstars. NASCAR has its short-track rivalries and championship drama. IndyCar has the Indianapolis 500.

IMSA offers something different: a blend of prototype machinery, production-based sports cars and endurance racing that rewards both individual speed and team execution.

The Rolex 24 at Daytona and the Mobil 1 Twelve Hours of Sebring are marquee events. Petit Le Mans has built its own reputation as one of North America's great endurance races.

For fans who enjoy the technical side of motorsports, the manufacturer rivalries are a major attraction. For casual viewers, the sight and sound of different classes sharing a circuit creates a spectacle that is difficult to replicate.

And for drivers, the challenge extends beyond simply being fast. Traffic management, pit strategy, changing conditions and communication can decide everything.

The series does not need to imitate NASCAR or Formula 1 to grow. It needs to show more people what makes it special.

The 2026 finale gave fans a historic Porsche victory, a Cadillac championship and 10 hours of racing at one of America's most beloved circuits.

That is a pretty compelling advertisement for sports-car racing.

The next challenge is turning those moments into lasting momentum — introducing new fans to the drivers, explaining the different classes and making the championship battles easier to follow.

Because once fans understand what is happening, IMSA has plenty to keep them watching.

Let's hear it: Is IMSA the most underrated major racing series in America? Or does another form of motorsports deserve that crown?

articles.title: NASCAR MEDIA FELL FOR @WhatsUndersteer’s TRAP, BUT THE INFAMOUS TROLL WAS RIGHT ABOUT KYLE LARSON AND COREY DAY ALL ALONG
articles.summary: The internet owes @WhatsUndersteer an apology. Well, maybe not an apology. But perhaps a small trophy, a microphone and a seat at the motorsports table. The...
articles.body:
The internet owes @WhatsUndersteer an apology.

Well, maybe not an apology. But perhaps a small trophy, a microphone and a seat at the motorsports table.

The infamous racing troll has made a name for himself online, and his unwavering belief in Kyle Larson and Corey Day has occasionally made him a target of NASCAR Twitter's collective eye-roll.

But what if the joke was on everyone else?

What if @WhatsUndersteer was not simply trolling the NASCAR community? What if he was trying to tell everyone something they were not ready to hear?

Larson has spent years making the argument for him.

The two-time NASCAR Cup Series champion is not merely a stock-car driver who occasionally hops into a dirt car for fun. He is one of the most accomplished crossover talents in modern American motorsports.

Sprint cars demand an entirely different set of instincts. Drivers manage enormous power, shifting grip and constant car rotation while fighting for inches on dirt tracks that can change dramatically throughout a race.

Larson has repeatedly demonstrated that those skills translate.

In July 2024, he beat Corey Day in the Front Row Challenge at Southern Iowa Speedway after starting 13th. Day pushed him hard enough to make the finish a genuine fight.

That was not just another Larson victory. It was a glimpse of the next generation chasing one of dirt racing's biggest talents.

And Larson's success in NASCAR has not diminished his standing in sprint-car racing. If anything, his willingness to compete across disciplines has strengthened his reputation.

Here is where the @WhatsUndersteer argument gets particularly interesting.

Day is not simply a prospect who looks fast on dirt. He has been making the difficult transition into NASCAR's national ranks while continuing to demonstrate why Hendrick Motorsports invested in his potential.

In April 2026, Day earned his first NASCAR O'Reilly Auto Parts Series victory at Talladega Superspeedway in his 22nd start. It was a major milestone for a young driver learning a completely different style of racing.

The victory also underscored an important point: Raw talent is only the beginning. Translating that talent into stock-car results takes experience, discipline and the ability to adapt.

Larson understands that process better than almost anyone. He has served as a sounding board for Day as the younger driver learns to navigate the demands of a major NASCAR organization.

The ceiling is exciting. The development is still underway.

And if you have watched Day compete in sprint cars, you can understand why people are paying attention.

This is the beautiful irony of motorsports social media.

A provocative account makes a claim. People react. The debate becomes about the person making the argument rather than the racing talent being discussed.

Suddenly, everyone is arguing about the troll instead of examining the drivers.

We cannot establish that @WhatsUndersteer deliberately engineered a media trap. But the broader point stands: An obnoxious messenger can still make a compelling argument.

Larson's accomplishments are real. Day's progress is real. Their shared dirt-racing background is real.

You do not have to endorse every post, every take or every stunt from a racing account to recognize when its central argument deserves consideration.

Sometimes the timeline gets distracted by the noise and misses the point.

Now comes the take that will really get NASCAR Twitter talking.

Sprint-car drivers might be the best all-around racers in the world.

Think about what the discipline demands. Drivers must manage slides, read changing track conditions, make split-second decisions and control a car that is constantly moving beneath them.

Larson has won at the highest level of NASCAR while remaining a formidable dirt racer. Tony Stewart built a championship career across IndyCar and NASCAR after developing his skills in open-wheel and dirt racing. Christopher Bell also carried a strong dirt-racing background into NASCAR's national spotlight.

That does not prove sprint-car drivers are objectively superior to Formula 1, IndyCar or sports-car specialists. Each discipline demands different skills, and the greatest drivers deserve credit for mastering their own environments.

But sprint-car racing develops an unusually broad set of car-control instincts. When those instincts meet the right equipment, coaching and opportunity, the results can be spectacular.

And when it comes to Larson and Day, the comparison is especially fascinating.

One is already a proven champion. The other is still building his résumé.

Both have dirt-track roots. Both have demonstrated serious ability. And both offer a reminder that some of racing's most exciting talents are developed far away from the bright lights of Sunday afternoon Cup racing.

Maybe the biggest troll move of all was making people angry enough to overlook the racing argument.

Larson has already established himself as one of the sport's most versatile talents. Day has taken a major step forward with his first O'Reilly Series win and has the resources of Hendrick Motorsports behind him.

Nobody can guarantee that Day will match Larson's career. Nobody can definitively crown sprint-car racers the greatest drivers on the planet, either.

But dismissing the talent pipeline that produced these two would be a mistake.

So let the timeline argue. Let the quote posts fly. Let the dirt-track faithful defend their guys.

At the end of the day, @WhatsUndersteer might just have earned the most unlikely title on racing Twitter.

And if Kyle Larson keeps winning and Corey Day keeps developing, that infamous account may have the last laugh.

Agree or disagree: Do sprint-car drivers make the best racers in the world? And is @WhatsUndersteer secretly one of the smartest accounts on NASCAR Twitter?

He has defended Larson and Day like no other. In our opinion, he may have been right all along.

articles.title: Alex Dunne: Irish Formula 2 title hopeful completes IndyCar test
articles.summary: Formula 2 title challenger Alex Dunne completes an IndyCar test in Alabama as he contemplates a move to the USA in 2027.
articles.body:
Formula 2 title challenger Alex Dunne has completed an IndyCar test in Alabama as he contemplates a move to the USA in 2027.

Ireland's Dunne is an Alpine junior driver and is in a three-way fight for the title in Formula 2, which supports Formula 1 on Grand Prix weekends.

The 20-year-old has one win and nine podiums in his second F2 season and is 18 points behind F1-bound leader Rafael Camara - with two more rounds scheduled in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

But with seats in F1 limited for 2027, Dunne tested an IndyCar for Dale Coyne Racing at Barber Motorsports Park on Monday.

He has also been linked to a third season in F2 as he chases his Formula 1 dream, but if he wins the championship he cannot return to the series next year.

Dunne posted the fastest time in a morning session which included American-born Conor Daly, who is the son of Irish former Formula 1 driver Derek.

Dale Coyne Racing have not announced their driver plans for 2027, and American teenager Nikita Johnson tested alongside Dunne on Monday.

"The car, the track, everything. I loved it all," Dunne told American outlet RACER. , external

"To be honest, the car was super cool. I think it's definitely got quite a bit more power, a lot more downforce than what I'm used to.

"To jump in and be comfortable pretty quickly, and I think I was quickest when I when I got out of the car in the morning, I really enjoyed it."

Dunne wins in Baku to surge into F2 title race

Brazilian Camara to join Haas for F1 debut in 2027

IndyCar is the leading open-wheel racing series in the USA, and ex-Formula 1 drivers such as Mick Schumacher, Marcus Ericsson and Romain Grosjean all raced in the series last year.

The biggest IndyCar race is the Indianapolis 500, which takes place every May in front of more than 230,000 spectators and is considered one of motorsport's 'Triple Crown' events, alongside Formula 1's Monaco Grand Prix and the Le Mans 24 Hours endurance race.

Britain's Louis Foster will drive for Rahal Letterman Lanigan Racing for the full 2027 campaign, while Katherine Legge and Jack Harvey both raced at the Indy 500 last year in one-off outings.

With the success of Spanish five-time IndyCar champion Alex Palou, the 2027 calendar will return to Europe with a round in Barcelona in July, and the rest of the season takes place on street courses, ovals and more traditional circuits in the USA and Canada.

Despite having only one morning testing in an IndyCar, Dunne said he "definitely likes what I've seen so far" and it was a series that had always interested him.

"I think naturally, with the path that I've been on and what I've worked towards, the goal will always be to be a Formula 1 driver," he said.

"I think there comes a time when, realistically, that chance becomes more difficult, and I've always said that the next best option for me and the thing I'd love to do most has always been IndyCar."

Portadown's Adam Carroll was the last driver from the island of Ireland to drive in IndyCar, when he competed in two races in 2010.

articles.title: Cristóbal Rosaleny, sobre Alonso y Sainz: "No sé muy bien cómo aguantan este año"
articles.standfirst: El especialista de Fórmula 1 analiza en La Tribu el gran momento del piloto de Mercedes, que podría proclamarse campeón del mundo en México, y la complicada situación de los españoles
articles.summary: El especialista de Fórmula 1 analiza en La Tribu el gran momento del piloto de Mercedes, que podría proclamarse campeón del mundo en México, y la complicada situación de los españoles
articles.body: Kimi Antonelli está a un paso de proclamarse campeón del mundo de Fórmula 1. El italiano, que acaba de cumplir 20 años, podría conquistar el título este fin de semana en el Gran Premio de México, después de su victoria en Austin. Una situación que ha analizado Cristóbal Rosaleny en La Tribu de Radio MARCA, durante su conversación con Raúl Varela, en la que ha destacado el acierto de Toto Wolff al apostar por el joven piloto como sustituto de Lewis Hamilton. "La verdad es que sí y yo fui uno de ellos, no lo niego", ha reconocido Rosaleny sobre quienes cuestionaron aquella decisión. "No tenía experiencia, porque había hecho una temporada en Fórmula 2 francamente mediocre, porque tenía en fin apenas tres años de experiencia en monoplazas", ha recordado. Sin embargo, el rendimiento del italiano ha terminado dando la razón a Mercedes. "Veinte recién cumplidos y esta misma semana muy probablemente campeón del mundo de Fórmula 1", ha destacado el especialista, que considera prácticamente imposible que Antonelli deje escapar el título. Más allá de los resultados, Cristóbal Rosaleny ha querido poner en valor el rendimiento del italiano frente a su compañero de equipo, George Russell. "Es que éste corre, corre de verdad al margen de que efectivamente el Mercedes pueda ser el mejor coche", ha asegurado. El especialista ha recordado la diferencia entre ambos pilotos en Austin: "Russell estuvo en la misma carrera que él, tenía el mismo coche que él y sin embargo terminó a más de 50 segundos". "Por tanto tiene un mérito especialísimo lo que está consiguiendo Kimi Antonelli, aunque es obvio también que no estamos viendo la mejor versión de un Russell que está condicionado, me atrevo a decir, mentalmente", ha añadido. Rosaleny también ha advertido de que el británico podría afrontar una temporada decisiva en 2027. "El año que viene es la segunda oportunidad y la última para un piloto top que quiere seguir siéndolo", ha señalado. La situación de los pilotos españoles también ha tenido protagonismo en La Tribu. Fernando Alonso y Carlos Sainz vivieron un complicado Gran Premio de Estados Unidos, marcado por los incidentes sufridos en los primeros compases de la carrera. "Tuvieron un gran premio terrible, los coches no les acompañaron en absoluto, pero sobre todo los dos recibieron golpes de otros rivales", ha explicado Rosaleny. El especialista ha detallado que Sainz sufrió el incidente en la salida, mientras que Alonso recibió un golpe de Alex Albon durante la primera vuelta. Ambos tuvieron que sustituir sus alerones delanteros y sufrieron daños adicionales. Una situación que ha llevado a Rosaleny a expresar su frustración por la temporada de los dos españoles: "No sé muy bien cómo aguantan este año. Se les está haciendo larguísimo y a nosotros también. Que pase ya por favor". La Fórmula 1 regresará este fin de semana con el Gran Premio de México, donde Antonelli tendrá su primera oportunidad de proclamarse campeón del mundo.

articles.body: dos puntos. Eso es lo que necesita Kimi Antonelli para terminar de batir a su compañero, George Russell, y arrebatarle el título por el que lleva tanto tiempo trabajando. Tras su salto ala F1 en 2019 con Williams, Russell ha buscado seguir mejorando para llegar a la posición en la que ha estado esta temporada: luchar por el Mundial de F1. Sin embargo, lo que no se esperaba el británico era que le saldría un competidor y el cual le pondría en tan serios aprietos, pues Kimi Antonelli está a un paso de hacer historia y convertirse en el Campeón del Mundo más joven de la F1. Lo que comenzó siendo como el perfecto "cuento de hadas" en dónde Russell se permitía soñar con una temporada perfecta, pues por fin tenía un arma con la que luchar. Un cambio de reglamento que claramente jugó a favor de Mercedes al adaptarse mejor que el resto de equipos y desarrollar un coche lo suficientemente aceptable como para, no sólo ganar, sino machacar a sus contrincantes. Y así pues, lo que se venía diciendo durante toda la pretemporada, e incluso finales de la temporada anterior, 2025, sobre Mercedes, Russell lo confirmó en el Primer Gran Premio en Australia. El británico se llevó la victoria de forma bastante holgada: casi tres segundos sobre su compañero, Kimi Antonelli, y más de 15 sobre el tercero, Charles Leclerc. Así pues, dimos por cerrada la temporada que apenas había empezado y escribimos su nombre en el Trofeo de Campeones mucho antes de lo que debimos, pues Mercedes no tenía rival y Antonelli aún estaba "aprendiendo". Con Ferrari siendo el posible rival a batir, pero sin que éstos tuvieran la solidez suficiente como para plantarles cara, añadido a los claros problemas que Red Bull y McLaren atravesaban, el camino hacia el título estaba despejado para Russell. Sin embargo, su "escudero" se reveló y ganó su primera carrera, y la segunda, y la tercera, y así hasta la 9ª recientemente conseguida en EEUU. A Russell le había salido un enemigo. El peor que podía tener y, sin lugar a duda, el más fuerte, pues luchaba con sus mismas armas. Sumado, además a los malos resultados que él mismo empezaba a firmar, tan sólo 8 pódiums y 3 victorias, frente a los 15 pódiums y 9 victorias de su compañero, han resultado en una diferencia de 123 puntos entre ambos pilotos de Mercedes al finalizar EEUU y el fin de un sueño que podría haberse hecho realidad esta temporada. El primer 'Match Ball' para el italiano se daba este fin de semana en Austin. Sin embargo, la carambola debía ser muy grande, aunque no imposible, para que se diese. Es más, por una posición Antonelli no pudo sentenciar el Mundial en COTA. No obstante, el italiano le sacó una ventaja de 54 segundos a Russell, quien terminó la carrera 8º. En definitiva, una diferencia abisma tratándose del mismo coche. Aun así, la carrera que vivió Russell resume su temporada a la perfección. "El ritmo fue pésimo. Eso es, en pocas palabras", decía el de Mercedes al acabar la carrera en Sky Sports F1. Y es que, el británico no consigue sacar el máximo potencial a su monoplaza tal y como Kimi sí es capaz de hacer. Tras cada carrera, Russell se llena de autocrítica y declara no ser lo suficientemente rápido, y ya no sólo contra su compañero de equipo, sino contra otros rivales que a lo largo de la temporada han ido mejorando. Los Ferrari estaban desde un principio y poco a poco se han ido sumando, McLaren primero y poco después, Red Bull. Por lo tanto, cada fin de semana se vuelve un tormento para Russell, quien lo describe así, en referencia a esta carrera, pero que podría aplicarse perfectamente a la gran parte de su temporada: "La penalización de cinco segundos no ayudó en nada y probablemente me costó dos o tres posiciones, pero el ritmo no fue lo suficientemente bueno cuando hacía falta. Simplemente no he sido lo suficientemente rápido". Sin embargo, no todo fue autocritica, pues el británico sabe que algo sucede con su monoplaza que no le deja firmar resultados similares a los que han llevado a Kimi a estar a un paso de coronarse Campeón del Mundo: "Tengo que intentar entender por qué ha sido así. Es extraño cuando estás tan lejos. Espero que haya alguna respuesta por ahí, pero de momento no la tengo".

articles.title: United States GP: Martin Brundle's verdict on 'outstanding' Kimi Antonelli win in Austin and Oscar Piastri's struggles in 2026 F1 cars
articles.summary: Sky Sports F1's Martin Brundle gives his verdict on Kimi Antonelli's "outstanding" performance which puts him on the brink of becoming F1's youngest world champion and the struggles for McLaren's Oscar Piastri and Mercedes' George Russell
articles.body:
His Austin qualifying and race performances demolished that concern in the most comprehensive way.

From seemingly nowhere, he produced a stormer of an initial time in the third and final top-10 shootout to secure pole position and deny Max Verstappen's Red Bull and the two Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, all of whom had seemed likely to beat him. It was his seventh pole of the season but his first since Spa back in the summer eight races ago, and therefore very timely.

Kimi produced a perfect start and opening lap to comfortably lead, while the slow-starting Verstappen had to fend off the Ferraris. His pace, consistency, and tyre management thereafter was simply outstanding.

Both Red Bull drivers, Verstappen and Isack Hadjar, had impressively made it through to Q3 having used only one set of soft tyres up to that point. This would give Max on the front row two brand new sets of soft tyres for the race, surely a significant advantage? As it turns out, not so, as they didn't last particularly well, forcing Max to pit first of everyone on Lap 13 of 56, and clearly now on a two-stop strategy.

Mercedes didn't panic or respond, they trusted their data and instincts, and their championship-leading driver, to babysit his tyres at sufficient pace to make only one pit stop on Lap 24.

With fresh tyres Max was inevitably very fast, and it initially appeared that he would be able to make up the extra 20 seconds he must spend in the pitlane for his second stop on Lap 31. But he couldn't clear the traffic with much ease. With his radio failing for the second time, but not before he would castigate his team for not moving his team-mate on a different run plan out of the way much sooner, he ended up a fairly disgruntled third.

I did the post-race interviews and Max did though beam a nice smile when I complimented him on his overtake of Lando Norris up into Turn 1. It was pure Verstappen, just as he looked highly likely to lose a position to Leclerc, he converted that into an overtake of the McLaren with a stunning and controlled slice while extremely late on the brakes.

It didn't do him much good in the end though because after Leclerc's own first stop on Lap 15, and having already been awesome on the opening lap of the race, he was mighty fast all the way to the chequered flag for a very well-earned second place.

Ferrari had led all three practice sessions and so their qualifying had been a relative disappointment, but Hamilton too was rapid in the closing stages and would finish fourth just a second behind Verstappen. Another lap and he'd have joined his team-mate Leclerc on the podium.

Norris did a fine job in fifth, having pitted on Lap 16 but then changing to a one-stopper, stretching his hard compound tyres a full 40 laps. In the end, he ran out of grip and slipped from second place, but it was good while it lasted.

Piastri struggling with 2026 cars and Russell's 'harsh' penalty

Oscar Piastri in the sister McLaren had another disappointing race, lacking front-running pace from relatively early on and finishing 52 seconds behind the winner. Oscar simply can't seem to gel with the 2026 cars and it's painful to witness after his stellar run last year.

Piastri's struggles would heavily impact another driver having a season to forget in the shape of George Russell. On the opening lap Russell was both attacking Hadjar's slow-starting Red Bull and defending from Piastri. He ran wide at the Turn 12 hairpin at the end of the back straight and rejoined, marginally ahead of Piastri. The Stewards looked at all the camera angles and data and decided that Russell had gained a lasting advantage off the track by not losing a place to Piastri, but given it was the opening lap and the proximity of other cars, they served him half the normal 10-second penalty in mitigation. I thought that was harsh, George felt somewhat more strongly about it.

Taking his five-second penalty at the first pit stop put him behind Piastri, and despite very solid initial pace on fresh tyres he simply couldn't find a way past the young Aussie and finished a full 54 seconds behind his winning team-mate in eighth place. Ouch.

Liam Lawson drove very well again for two points at Racing Bulls in ninth and Pierre Gasly grabbed the final point for Alpine in 10th, the position he started.

Nico Hulkenberg finished 11th and just out of the points - that's Audi's 10th race this year when just missing out. That's a torment which revives bad memories for me, back when points only went down to sixth place, I had a spate of dragging some reluctant machine past all the accidents and unreliability to finish a point-less seventh.

Antonelli's supreme victory ensures he will be the youngest ever F1 world champion by over three years, usurping Sebastian Vettel. And the first Italian F1 world champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953, despite such motorsport passion and history in that country.

Verstappen is now out of championship contention, incredibly for the first time since 2020. Russell and Hamilton would have to win every race until the end of the year, with Antonelli not showing up, for them to be champion. It's a case of when, and not if.

Austin put on at great show at COTA, a combined 460,000 fans had all the usual great views along with live music, fun fairs, and many other attractions, and a spectacular hospitality suite and infinity pool at the very top of the already high first corner. The lucky few were transported over the track in gondolas on ski-slope-style pylons and cables, I'm impressed by how F1 keeps developing as a full experience, even though the race didn't turn out to be a classic.

articles.title: Andrea Valero, de MADRING: “El motor ha salido de la pista y ha salido incluso del circuito”
articles.standfirst: La responsable de patrocinios del GP de España de F1, el de MotoGP y el de contenido de DAZN analizan cómo las nuevas audiencias y los contenidos digitales están transformando el negocio del motor
articles.summary: La responsable de patrocinios del GP de España de F1, el de MotoGP y el de contenido de DAZN analizan cómo las nuevas audiencias y los contenidos digitales están transformando el negocio del motor
articles.body: La Fórmula 1 y MotoGP atraviesan un momento de enorme crecimiento, con nuevos aficionados, nuevos mercados y un atractivo comercial que va mucho más allá de lo que sucede sobre el asfalto. Una transformación que fue protagonista en la mesa ‘La nueva era del motor en el siglo XXI, expectativas y futuro’, celebrada durante el encuentro El futuro de las retransmisiones deportivas, organizado por MARCA y DAZN. Un coloquio que reunió a Andrea Valero, Head of Sponsorship de MADRING y del Gran Premio de España de Fórmula 1; Borja de Altolaguirre, Head of Sponsorship de MotoGP Sports Entertainment Group; y Quim Domènech, Executive Vice President Global Content & Editorial de DAZN, que analizaron las claves del crecimiento del motor y los desafíos que plantea su expansión internacional. Uno de los principales asuntos abordados fue precisamente cómo el motor ha conseguido trascender la competición para convertirse en un fenómeno social y cultural. Una evolución que Andrea Valero considera fundamental para entender el interés creciente de los patrocinadores. “El motor ha salido de la pista y ha salido incluso del circuito. Hoy en día el interés del aficionado está en las historias que hay detrás, en las rivalidades, en los equipos”, explicó la responsable de MADRING, que destacó cómo la Fórmula 1 ha conseguido conectar con otros sectores. “Ya no competimos solo en lo que es deporte, sino que la industria del motor se posiciona como una plataforma social, una plataforma cultural que conecta gastronomía, turismo, moda y música”, añadió. Un fenómeno que se refleja también en el perfil de los aficionados. Según los datos de Fórmula 1, el 42% de su audiencia global está formada por mujeres, una transformación que está abriendo las puertas a nuevos patrocinadores y formas de consumir la competición. “La Fórmula 1 ya no solo se consume durante la carrera, sino que se consume durante todo el año y ha pasado a ser un tema frecuente de conversación social”, señaló Valero. Una tendencia que considera especialmente importante para las marcas, que ahora encuentran oportunidades para conectar con públicos mucho más amplios que los tradicionales aficionados al motor. El estreno del Gran Premio de España de Fórmula 1 en Madrid fue uno de los principales ejemplos utilizados durante el coloquio. La primera edición de MADRING cerró con 352.618 asistencias acumuladas durante las cuatro jornadas del evento, una cifra que refleja su capacidad de convocatoria, pero también la dimensión del proyecto desde el punto de vista comercial. “Hemos congregado a más de 352.000 personas en las gradas y en nuestros espacios de hospitality”, destacó Andrea Valero. Pero el objetivo de MADRING no se limita al fin de semana de carreras. La intención de sus responsables es aprovechar el atractivo de la Fórmula 1 para construir una marca que mantenga su actividad durante todo el año y que permita a los patrocinadores desarrollar experiencias y contenidos más allá de la competición. “El foco y el objetivo de MADRING es ir más allá del fin de semana de la carrera. Por eso surge MADRING como marca comercial y como una plataforma que puede generar contenido durante todo el año”, explicó. En este sentido, Valero también desveló la dimensión comercial que ha alcanzado el proyecto en su primera edición. “Hemos conseguido casi 40 marcas que han estado con nosotros y con las que hemos hecho acuerdos locales”, aseguró. Una cifra que, según explicó, ha sido posible gracias a la colaboración con Fórmula 1, que ha permitido desarrollar licencias, productos de merchandising, contenidos y nuevas experiencias para los aficionados. “La colaboración que hemos tenido ha sido muy positiva y ha permitido que creemos ese modelo comercial que tenemos hoy en día, que hace que todo el engranaje funcione”, destacó. La repercusión digital ha sido otro de los grandes indicadores del éxito del Gran Premio. Valero señaló que el fin de semana de MADRING generó más de cinco millones de interacciones en redes sociales, una muestra del alcance de un acontecimiento que atrajo a personalidades del deporte, la música y el entretenimiento. “El impacto televisivo siempre es uno de los más potentes, pero está muy igualado con la cobertura mediática y el contenido digital”, afirmó. Una exposición que supone un valor añadido para los patrocinadores y que permite que el retorno comercial vaya mucho más allá de las audiencias de televisión. Quim Domènech también quiso destacar la dimensión que había alcanzado la primera edición de MADRING. El directivo de DAZN puso como ejemplo la presencia de jugadores del Real Madrid, celebridades e influencers, que contribuyeron a multiplicar la conversación alrededor del Gran Premio. “Estamos hablando de un evento deportivo, que es una carrera, pero estamos hablando de un evento cultural”, explicó. Una repercusión que, a su juicio, sería difícil de conseguir mediante campañas publicitarias convencionales y que demuestra el valor que generan los grandes acontecimientos deportivos. El crecimiento internacional también está marcando la estrategia de MotoGP. Borja de Altolaguirre destacó la oportunidad que representa la llegada de Liberty Media, que está trasladando al Mundial de motociclismo parte de las estrategias que han contribuido a la expansión de otras grandes competiciones deportivas. El campeonato cuenta con una base global de 632 millones de aficionados, según los datos correspondientes a 2025, y ha experimentado un importante crecimiento tanto en la asistencia a los circuitos como en las audiencias televisivas. Especialmente significativo es el comportamiento de las carreras al sprint, cuya audiencia aumentó un 26% respecto al año anterior. Unas cifras que, para Altolaguirre, demuestran que existe un enorme potencial de crecimiento en nuevos mercados sin perder el arraigo histórico de MotoGP en países como España o Italia y en regiones como el sudeste asiático. Sin embargo, uno de los principales desafíos es conseguir que los aficionados mantengan su vínculo con el campeonato una vez que termina el Gran Premio de su país. “Lo que tenemos que hacer es convertir esas 22 carreras en plataformas de marketing durante todo el año”, explicó el responsable de patrocinios de MotoGP. Para conseguirlo, el campeonato está impulsando nuevas experiencias, eventos en las ciudades y actividades que permitan mantener el contacto con los aficionados durante los meses en los que no hay competición en sus respectivos países. “Tenemos que ayudar a los promotores a tener contenido, experiencias y eventos para que el aficionado que ha venido a MotoGP no se quede desenganchado hasta el año siguiente”, señaló Altolaguirre. Una estrategia que busca combinar la dimensión global del campeonato con la identidad local de cada carrera. “Queremos que cuando vayas a Australia, Malasia o Jerez tengas MotoGP, pero que sea muy distinto ir a un sitio o a otro”, explicó, defendiendo que cada Gran Premio ofrezca una experiencia propia y diferenciada. La transformación del consumo audiovisual fue otro de los grandes temas de la mesa. Quim Domènech defendió que las nuevas formas de seguir el deporte no deben entenderse como una amenaza para las retransmisiones tradicionales, sino como una oportunidad para ampliar las audiencias y atraer a nuevos espectadores. “Los nuevos tipos de consumo no suplen a los anteriores, sino que forman parte de un nuevo escenario, de un nuevo ecosistema”, aseguró el ejecutivo de DAZN. En este sentido, destacó que la calidad de las retransmisiones en directo sigue siendo fundamental, pero que los contenidos que se generan alrededor de cada carrera tienen un alcance cada vez mayor. “Si empezamos a sumar a nivel de redes sociales toda la audiencia que tenemos en los posts, multiplica al evento deportivo en directo”, explicó. Una circunstancia que obliga a las plataformas a adaptar su estrategia para atender tanto a los aficionados que siguen íntegramente las carreras como a aquellos que prefieren consumir momentos concretos, resúmenes o historias que se viralizan en el entorno digital. Para responder a estos nuevos hábitos, DAZN está desarrollando formatos que permiten acceder al contenido deportivo de diferentes maneras. Uno de ellos es Moments, un formato de vídeos verticales dentro de la propia plataforma, pensado para que los usuarios puedan consumir de forma rápida los momentos más destacados de una competición. “Es un feed vertical de grandes momentos de la carrera que ponemos inmediatamente a disposición en la plataforma”, explicó Domènech. La idea es que estos contenidos funcionen como una puerta de entrada para nuevos aficionados, pero también como un complemento para quienes ya siguen las carreras. “Puede funcionar porque simplemente quieres ver cómo ha ido la carrera y lo consumes de una forma diferente, o puede ayudar a que después te veas el evento porque ha habido algo interesante o te plantees ver la siguiente carrera”, apuntó. Domènech también destacó la importancia de mantener un equilibrio entre las audiencias tradicionales y los nuevos espectadores. La evolución de las retransmisiones ha permitido que los aficionados tengan cada vez más conocimientos técnicos sobre aspectos como la gestión de la energía en Fórmula 1 o la inclinación de las motos en las curvas. “Ahora tenemos una audiencia que sabe mucho más, que es muchísimo más experta, que se ha convertido en más mainstream y que además es muy fiel”, afirmó. El desafío, por tanto, es ofrecer contenidos capaces de satisfacer a los aficionados más especializados sin dificultar la entrada a quienes acaban de descubrir el deporte. El futuro comercial de la Fórmula 1 y MotoGP también pasa por cambiar la relación entre los patrocinadores y las competiciones. Ya no se trata únicamente de conseguir visibilidad a través de un logotipo o un anuncio durante la retransmisión, sino de integrar a las marcas en las experiencias que viven los aficionados. Desde MADRING, Andrea Valero defendió que el éxito de este nuevo modelo depende de la colaboración entre los organizadores de los grandes premios, los propietarios de los derechos y las plataformas audiovisuales. “La propiedad ayuda al promotor, el promotor prepara esos modelos comerciales y explota el circuito más allá de lo que es la carrera, lo integra con la ciudad y conecta con el destino. Luego el broadcaster es clave también para contar todo eso”, explicó. Una visión compartida por DAZN, que pretende ofrecer a los patrocinadores una presencia mucho más amplia dentro de su ecosistema de contenidos. “Queremos que las marcas sean parte del evento”, aseguró Domènech, que destacó las posibilidades de desarrollar formatos personalizados, contenidos bajo demanda, menciones durante las retransmisiones y activaciones digitales. Un modelo que refleja la transformación del negocio del motor. La carrera sigue siendo el principal atractivo, pero el crecimiento de la Fórmula 1 y MotoGP está cada vez más vinculado a su capacidad para generar historias, experiencias y contenidos que mantengan conectados a los aficionados durante todo el año. Una evolución que está llevando a las competiciones a convertirse en auténticas plataformas de entretenimiento global.

articles.title: Ferrari volvió a pifiarla
articles.standfirst: Un buen fin de semana no es sinónimo de una buena carrera
articles.summary: Un buen fin de semana no es sinónimo de una buena carrera
articles.body: Un fin de semana que podría haber sido la reivindicación de Ferrari y que, sin embargo, volvió a resultar en un autentico fiasco para los de Maranello. A pesar de haber dominado los tres Entrenamientos Libres que componen el fin de semana, posicionándose como claros favoritos para finiquitar en trabajo en lo más alto, a la hora de la verdad volvieron a meter la pata y acabar con un resultado inconformista. A esto se le añade la gran pérdida que supuso para el campeonato. Aunque Lewis Hamilton aún tenga oportunidad, matemáticamente hablando, de alzarse con el Título de F1, su gran fiasco este fin de semana en la carrera, anuló casi por completo sus posibilidades, sacándole Antonelli, además, los colores su equipo compatriota. El joven piloto de Mercedes supo gestionar bien el fin de semana y dar el mazazo final cuando había que hacerlo: en 'qualy' y carrera. Ante este nuevo fiasco por parte de Ferrari, su jefe de equipo, Fred Vasseur, ha tenido que salir a dar las explicaciones pertinentes ante tal resultado final, cuando venían "comiéndose" el fin de semana y apuntaban a un doblete. Según explica el francés, la actuación del SF-26 fue impecable durante el fin de semana, excepto en dos vueltas en concreto: "El problema es que hicimos todas las vueltas, desde las primeras en el FP1, hasta la última de la carrera, en un buen estado. Excepto las dos últimas de la Q3 en ambos coches, y es probablemente donde perdimos". Y es que, el problema vuelve a ser el mismo de siempre: el desaprovechamiento de las oportunidades que se les presentan y la incapacidad de mantener esa buena actuación, que pueden llegar a enseñar durante los entrenamientos, cuando la presión sube. "Creo que, tanto con el coche como con los neumáticos, la ventana es siempre muy estrecha y en cuanto te sales un poco, pierdes entre dos y tres décimas. En la F1 actual, esas dos o tres décimas pueden ser una 6ª posición. Esto significa que puedes ir de un gran resultado a ningún lugar por un simple ráfaga de aire o porque sencillamente has deslizado un poco más de lo normal", declaraba el francés. Ante estos pequeños errores que claramente les penalizan, Vasseur se pone deberes en la totalidad del equipo y en especial a sus pilotos. "Está claro que el ritmo estaba desde el primer momento en que el coche saltó a pista el viernes por la mañana. Pero tenemos que prestar atención es a que la competitividad no es sólo el paquete en su conjunto, sino también el 'set-up', la gestión de los neumáticos, saber si estás en una buena posición o si estás haciendo un buen fin de semana. Además, si tienes el paquete, pero no estás en la posición adecuada, tienes que tener ese tacto de que algo no está funcionando", sentenció Vasseur.

articles.title: Formula 1 next engine regulations to introduce V8 turbo hybrid engines
articles.summary: Formula 1's next engine regulations are set to introduce V8 turbo hybrid engines that are simplified and less expensive compared to the existing rules.
articles.body:
Formula 1's next engine regulations are set to introduce V8 turbo hybrid engines that are simplified and less expensive to make compared to the existing rules.

A proposal document sent by governing body the FIA to the six manufacturers in F1 outlines a framework for discussions on engines to be introduced in either 2030 or 2031.

Multiple sources within F1 have provided BBC Sport with the details within the document.

The plan, which comes after initial discussions with individual engine manufacturers on a one-to-one basis, proposes cheaper, lighter, simpler engines with a more visceral sound.

However, the FIA has moved away from its initial proposal to return to naturally aspirated engines.

The stated aim of the new rules is to introduce lighter, more responsive cars, increased emphasis on driver skill, relevant technologies, reduced cost, to make it easier for new manufacturers to enter F1 and to continue with the sport's commitment to reducing emissions.

This comes after criticism of the new engines introduced this year for their complexity and the way their design and operation has diminished the driving challenge of some of F1's best corners.

Will F1 go back to the future with its engines?

The engines used in F1 at the moment are 1.6-litre V6 turbos with a power split of 53-47 between the internal combustion engine and electrical components. This will be changed to 60-40 in two steps by 2028.

The FIA document proposes a V8 engine with a capacity of between 2-2.3-litres with a smaller turbo running at reduced boost pressure and a less powerful hybrid system.

The electrical motor would have a recovery capacity of 200kW compared to the current 350kW.

The idea is for 100kW (134bhp) of this to be available at all times, with a further 100kW to be used for a push-to-pass or overtake mode.

The rest of the total power output of in the region of 900bhp will be provided by the internal combustion engine.

F1 will continue with fully sustainable fuels but with the ambition to make the requirements around them less complex and therefore lower production costs.

The aim is to cut a total of 80kg from the overall weight of the cars.

The proposal changes the previous stance of the FIA on naturally aspirated engines - president Mohammed Ben Sulayem initially proposed a return of V10s at the start of last year and has more recently been pushing V8s.

The addition of the turbo satisfies the need for the engines to be road-relevant, as well as increasing efficiency and requiring less fuel than a pure naturally aspirated engine.

The published proposals can be seen as a kind of middle ground between Ben Sulayem's initial stance, the desire of at least some manufacturers to keep turbos and a significant hybrid element, and a recognition that the latest rules were flawed in concept and execution.

The new engines will have none of the problems of energy starvation about which drivers have complained this season.

Fernando Alonso has called F1 the "battery world championship" and described fast corners as "the charging station for the car", while Max Verstappen has described the new rules as "Formula E on steroids" and anti-racing.

Both have since tempered their criticisms having seen that the sport's bosses have listened to their comments on the engines and made immediate changes to the rules this year as well as started working towards a new direction in the future.

The fundamental framework of the proposal for the new engine's architecture is said to be basically acceptable to all the manufacturers.

However, the details around how the rules operate will need discussion.

The document outlines two possible ways forward for the new rule set.

One is aimed at minimising necessary adaptation - for example, a 2.1-litre V8 could be produced by simply adding two cylinders to the current 1.6-litre blocks and reducing the size of the turbo and MGU-K (hybrid motor).

The other, more controversial, is to have an external manufacturer design and supply a baseline power-unit with a high degree of standardisation, on to which manufacturers could add a degree of customisation.

However, insiders say the manufacturers are all aligned on wanting to design and build their own power-units and for engines to remain a performance differentiator.

The companies who currently supply engines to F1 teams are Mercedes, Ferrari, Audi, Honda and Red Bull. Cadillac, which entered F1 this year with its own team, is planning to produce an engine to the new rules.

There are two further arguments to steer away from the standardisation route:

The first is that the reasons for it - to safeguard against manufacturers leaving the sport - is irrelevant as all six will be committed under the new rule set.

The second is that the standardisation of electronics control units this season has led to a series of problems, such as at the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia when cars were restricted to not much more than walking pace because of a software bug.

The document outlines a proposal to cut the engine budget cap by 50% from the current level of $190m (£143m) per year.

However, this is considered a starting point for discussions, while there are also concerns about providing a suitable glide path down to the new number to enable teams to manage the impact on workforces.

Discussions around the budget cap also involve the need to balance ongoing development of the existing engines with design and construction of the new ones.

That topic is interlinked with whether the new rules will come into force in 2030 or 2031.

The existing contracts in F1 bind the FIA, teams and commercial rights holder together only until 2030.

Ben Sulayem has previously threatened to introduce his own rules unilaterally in 2031.

That threat appears to have receded and the process has been marked by a spirit of co-operation, which is expected to continue.

An FIA spokesperson declined to comment on or discuss the document, pointing instead to an Instagram post published on Ben Sulayem's account outlining the aims and objectives of of the new rules. , external It makes no mention of turbos or hybrid technology.

The aim is for discussions over the next weeks to lead to a proposal that can be put to F1's legislative body, the FIA world council, in December.

articles.title: George Russell: Toto Wolff rejects Helmut Marko's doubts over Mercedes driver's future hopes as Kimi Antonelli nears title
articles.summary: Former Red Bull chief Helmut Marko has cast doubt over George Russell's hopes of becoming F1 world champion in the future; Toto Wolff says the Brit has what is required to win a title; watch every session of the Mexico City GP from this Friday, live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
Antonelli won the United States Grand Prix on Sunday to move to the brink of being crowed the sport's youngest ever champion, with the 20-year-old only needing to finish ninth this weekend in the Mexico City Grand Prix to seal the title with four rounds to spare.

Perhaps the most shocking element of the Italian's historic campaign has been the way he has outperformed Russell, who had begun the season as the clear title favourite after dominating Antonelli during the latter's rookie season last year.

Speaking ahead of Sunday's race in Austin, former Red Bull motorsport advisor Marko told Sky Germany : "Mentally, it's certainly a massive setback and it's a blow. Russell is no longer the number one driver."

"Antonelli has quite clearly taken that spot from him. But Russell is one of the top drivers. I doubt whether he'll ever have another chance at the world title or be given number one status anywhere."

Asked after Sunday's race whether he has a response to Marko's comments on Russell's title pedigree, Wolff said: "I start with Helmut. I mean, he's my Austrian… not so buddy, but I respect his opinion.

"But I think he's wrong on George. George has all the ability. I think the car doesn't suit him.

"I think that at the beginning of the season, it's maybe difficult to cope with a situation where you're feeling like this is my year to come, and then you have this wunderkind on the other side that starts to really chip away.

"And I believe that in a new season, George, if we provide him a quick car, it's absolutely possible, (he) has absolutely what it takes to win a championship.

"So, I think it's a bit too easy to say, let's forget about all these years where he won in F2 and in F3 in his rookie years and the European championships back-to-back in karting. That's still all there."

'George is not three tenths slower than Kimi'

Russell had performed with great consistency since joining Mercedes for the 2022 season, exceeding expectations by impressing with Lewis Hamilton as his team-mate for his first three years with the Silver Arrows.

His strong form continued in 2025 as Russell maximised an underperforming car to finish fourth in the Drivers' Championship, more than doubling the points total of seventh-placed Antonelli.

It therefore came as a major surprise when, after Russell won the season opener in Australia, Antonelli reeled off the first five wins of his career in succession to establish a championship lead that he has never looked like relinquishing.

Wolff believes the major regulation change that preceded the 2026 season is the main reason for Russell's struggles, but says it is on the team to help the 28-year-old rediscover his best form.

"George, for all of us in the team, is a champion and has won in every category," Wolff said. "And I think he merits to be put in the group of the very best ones (drivers). We've seen that last year.

"And this year, we've seen this variability in results. When we land the car in the way that suits him, he's absolutely fast. But when it drops out of that operational window, he struggles, and he struggles more than maybe Kimi.

"And that is on us. We just have to work it out with him how there can be such a difference in driving, in performance, because George is not half a second slower, three tenths slower than Kimi. That's just absolutely not the case.

"So, what is it that he doesn't like? What is it that we need to do in terms of modifying the car, setting it up in a different way for him to go fast? Because it's all there, the intelligence, the ability, the determination."

articles.title: En Malasia se determinará el futuro de Qatar
articles.standfirst: Los pilotos de MotoGP preparan una nueva reunión en Sepang para decidir qué sucede con el Gran Premio de Qatar
articles.summary: Los pilotos de MotoGP preparan una nueva reunión en Sepang para decidir qué sucede con el Gran Premio de Qatar
articles.body: La inestabilidad geopolítica, y sus catastróficas consecuencias, son las que ponen en entredicho la celebración final del Gran Premio de Qatar, dentro de poco más de dos semanas. Y es que, ante la insistencia por parte del campeonato en declararlo un lugar seguro donde desarrollar la actividad, los pilotos no están del todo de acuerdo y buscarán este fin de semana tomar una decisión. Tal y cómo sucedió en Phillip Island, la parrilla de MotoGP celebrará una reunión esta semana en Sepang con el fin de ponerse de acuerdo y determinar qué hacer finalmente con el Gran Premio de Qatar pues saben de la importancia que tienen sus decisiones en el campeonato y no todos ven prudente viajar a un país que, de forma indirecta, está sumido en una guerra. Durante la primera reunión celebrada en Australia, hubo una gran mayoría que se negaba a correr en Qatar ante el más que evidente riesgo que supondría. 15 pilotos frente a los 5 que votaron sí (4 Aprilias), y 2 abstenciones fueron los resultados que se sacaron de esta "primera vuelta". Sin embargo, la cancelación de las carreras en Australia por la falta de seguridad que suponía el temporal, según se declaró desde Dirección de Carrera, pone en entredicho las palabras del campeonato sobre la seguridad de Qatar. Tal y como muchos pilotos han comentado, si no era seguro correr en Australia, tampoco lo es correr en Qatar. Aun así, hubieron pilotos que votaron 'sí', aunque ante la situación actual del campeonato, los motivos no se necesitan explicar. La lesión del '89', claro contendiente al título, influye enormemente en la posición que adopten los de Noale, pues, aunque no haya ordenes de equipo, los cuatro integrantes de la marca saben exactamente qué deben hacer, por el bien de Aprilia. Es por ello que esos votos positivos, aunque sean pocos, son determinantes, pues para forzar la cancelación del Gran Premio por parte de los pilotos, debe haber unanimidad en la decisión que se tome. Carlos Ezpeleta, director deportivo de MotoGP, tiene planeado un viaje este miércoles 28 de octubre al país Qatarí con la intención de evaluar la situación por sí mismo y tomar finamente una decisión, algo que llevan pidiendo los pilotos y los equipos en general, ante la proximidad del Gran Premio Estados Unidos, Francia, España o Alemania son algunos de los muchos países que desaconsejan viajar a Qatar e incluso hacer escala, pues la situación demasiado inestable y podría escalar de forma inminente en cualquier momento, según aseguran desde los distintos Gobiernos.

articles.title: Bicampeón Kimi Antonelli
articles.standfirst: Con 20 años y 68 días se convertirá el domingo en el ganador más joven de la historia. Los cinco pilotos a los que supera tienen, como mínimo, dos títulos mundiales
articles.summary: Con 20 años y 68 días se convertirá el domingo en el ganador más joven de la historia. Los cinco pilotos a los que supera tienen, como mínimo, dos títulos mundiales
articles.body: “¡Dónde vas Fittipaldi!” Una de las frases más escuchadas en la España de los 70 y 80. Y es que el bravo Emerson fue un soplo de aire fresco para la Fórmula 1. En 1972 lograba convertirse en el campeón más joven de la historia con 25 años y 273 días. Pilotaba un Lotus. Luego llegaría otra corona más en 1974. Al Gran Circo se llegaba más tarde que ahora y como culminación de una carrera deportiva. No debutabas con 19 años en uno de los mejores equipos de la historia y después de un programa de test de 9.000 kilómetros. Se calcula que Mercedes ha invertido en la carrera de Antonelli 15 millones de euros. En los 70 no había telemetría, el riesgo de muerte era por desgracia muy real… Hemos pasado en medio siglo de ver a hombres jugándose la vida a casi adolescentes divirtiéndose. Que no corren cuando llueve. Viene Camara protegido por Ferrari, llegaron antes Bortoleto y Bearman. Esta tendencia empezó con un Verstappen que debutó siendo menor de edad. Cuarto piloto más joven de la historia en lograr su primer título con 24 años y 73 días. Lo hubiera sido antes de tener un coche dominante. Desde entonces, las escuderías grandes persiguen su mirlo blanco y barato que termine por jubilar a los mayores de la parrilla. A menos palmarés y popularidad, más riesgo de que te arrasen las nuevas generaciones, como ha pasado con el siempre rápido Ocon en Haas. Esteban cobraba y el brasileño Camara supondrá un descuento en los motores Ferrari y un polo de atracción para los patrocinadores de su país. Más allá de su calidad, demostrada en F-3, F-2, y batiéndose con Antonelli en las categorías inferiores. El tercero más precoz de la lista es Fernando Alonso. 24 años y 58 días tenía en Brasil 2005. Llegó a la Fórmula 1 sin test alguno. No había simuladores, sólo Play Station de baja definición para aprenderse los circuitos. Estuvo un año en el peor equipo, Minardi, otro de probador haciendo kilómetros con Renault y no tuvo un coche de verdad bueno hasta su quinto año. Briatore, su padrino deportivo, le hizo pasar una larga mili fuera de los circuitos. Kimi, debutante y derrotado por Russell sobre un coche que ganó dos carreras en 2025, es sólo un poco menos afortunado que el siguiente de esta lista de superélite, Lewis Hamilton. El inglés tuvo un coche imperial ya desde 2007. Y hubiera sido campeón de no tener enfrente a Alonso. Además, su McLaren perdió competitividad después de que su compañero dejara de trabajar en el monoplaza durante un verano al rojo vivo. Fernando se hartó de que su rival por el título se aprovechara de su experiencia y sus ideas para intentar ganarle. Como el británico, Antonelli es un fichaje infantil. Lewis llamó la atención de Ron Dennis con doce años y, desde entonces, disfrutó siempre de los mejores materiales en el karting. El joven de Bolonia llegó a conocer a Toto con sólo once primaveras, y después de haber sido rechazado por Ferrari. Volaba en los karts y Massimo Rivola, entonces jefe de la cantera roja, le dijo a Arrivabene que debían ficharle. Le pareció demasiado joven… Terminamos con el tetracampeón Vettel, discreto en su debut con un Williams BMW en Indianápolis, brillante en su primer año completo con un Toro Rosso al que llevó a la victoria bajo la lluvia en Monza… Terminó subcampeón con Red Bull en 2009, aunque siempre nos quedará la duda de qué hubiera pasado ese año si Alonso llega a firmar con ellos. Faltó el canto de un duro. Los famosos vasos comunicantes de las carreras. En Abu Dabi 2010, cuando Petrov le amargó el día a millones de españoles, ‘Seb’ tenía 23 años y 134 días. Como Kimi, supo adaptarse muy bien a un nuevo reglamento, el de los difusores soplados. Así las cosas, tengo la sensación de que el próximo campeón del mundo es el claro favorito para repetir título en 2027. Austin ha sido un duro golpe de realidad para sus incompletos rivales. El rumor del anterior periplo era que los motores Mercedes sufrían con las altas temperaturas de Malasia y Singapur, de ahí que le recuperación de Max nos hiciera creer en otra cosa. En una pista convencional y con la posibilidad de poder apretar el ‘grifo’ de la potencia, la pole se volvió a vestir de plata. Ferrari tiene un problema en calificación y de potencia, y el Red Bull es un coche delicado e irregular. Esta base recibirá mejoras aero y de motor para la temporada próxima. También la historia está del lado del joven italiano. Ninguno de los seis pilotos más precoces de siempre tiene menos de dos títulos mundiales. ¿Dónde estará su techo?
